Fulfilment writers answer that the 'latter days' are the days begun with Christ (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2), and that Jesus expressly told the Samaritan woman that worship would no longer be tied to 'this mountain' or Jerusalem (John 4:21-23). The law going out from Zion fits the apostolic mission, which Luke frames 'beginning from Jerusalem'. Amillennialists place full world peace in the new creation; postmillennialists expect it to grow through the gospel within history, as the kingdom spreads (Matthew 13:31-33).

Dispensationalists reply that the promise includes nations still learning and being judged (2:4), which fits a millennial age better than the eternal state, where no one needs arbitration. They argue that Hebrews 12:22 describes believers' present access to heaven, not a cancellation of the earthly Jerusalem's future role, and that Jesus himself spoke of Jerusalem's future 'until' the times of the Gentiles end (Luke 21:24).
A light to the nations

The Servant, whom God calls 'Israel' (Isaiah 49:3), is given a mission to raise up the tribes of Jacob and restore the preserved of Israel. God says that is too small a thing: he will also make the Servant a light to the nations, so that his salvation reaches the end of the earth (49:6).
God calls his Servant 'Israel', in whom he will be glorified, yet this Servant also restores Israel (49:5).
God's promise to Abraham that in him all families of the earth will be blessed is the root of Israel's calling to the nations.
Simeon takes the infant Jesus in the temple and calls him 'a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and the glory of your people Israel'.
At Pisidian Antioch, Paul and Barnabas quote Isaiah 49:6 and say 'the Lord has commanded us' with it, turning to the Gentiles.
Paul tells Agrippa that the Messiah, first to rise from the dead, would proclaim light both to the Jewish people and to the Gentiles.
A great multitude from every nation, tribe, people and language stands before the throne and the Lamb.

Isaiah 40-55 addresses the exiles in Babylon, promising return and naming Cyrus (Isaiah 44:28; 45:1). The return under Cyrus (538 BC) restored some of 'the preserved of Israel', but no light reached the nations in any great way. In the first century, synagogues across the Roman world drew Gentile God-fearers, and Paul's mission, beginning about AD 46-48 in Cyprus and Galatia (Acts 13-14), made this text his commission. By the time Paul wrote Romans (about AD 57) there were churches of Gentiles from Jerusalem to Illyricum (Romans 15:19).

The fulfilment reading holds that Jesus is the true Israel and the Servant who restores the remnant of Jacob and also lights the nations. Because the apostles apply the Servant's mission to themselves (Acts 13:47), the church shares in it: Jew and Gentile believers carry the light of Israel's Messiah to the end of the earth. Gentile Christians are therefore the fruit of Israel's calling, not outsiders to it.

Dispensationalists agree that the Servant is the Messiah and that the Gentile mission fulfils part of Isaiah 49:6. They stress that the restoration of 'the tribes of Jacob' (49:6) and the land (49:8, 'to establish the land, to apportion the desolate heritages') is still ahead. They expect national Israel, once converted, to be a light to the nations in the millennium (Isaiah 60:3; Zechariah 8:23, where ten men from the nations take hold of a Jew's robe).

Fulfilment writers reply that the restoration of Jacob's tribes began with Jesus' choice of the Twelve (Luke 22:30) and the thousands of Jews who believed (Acts 21:20). The land-apportioning image in 49:8 is quoted by Paul for the present day of salvation ('now is the day of salvation', 2 Corinthians 6:2 quoting Isaiah 49:8), so the passage's time is the gospel age. In Zechariah 8:23 the nations seek out the Jew because 'God is with you', which they see fulfilled when Gentiles came to Jewish apostles and their Messiah.

Dispensationalists answer that a present application does not exhaust a text: Paul can quote Isaiah 49:8 for today while the nation's land restoration still awaits. They argue that Romans 11:12 ('how much more their fullness') shows a greater blessing to the nations when Israel as a people turns to Christ.
'Not my people' called 'my people'

Hosea's children were named Lo-ruhamah ('no mercy') and Lo-ammi ('not my people') as signs of judgment on the northern kingdom (Hosea 1:6-9). Yet God promises that the number of Israel will be like the sand of the sea, and where it was said 'You are not my people', they will be called 'children of the living God' (1:10). Judah and Israel will be gathered under one head (1:11), and God will say to 'not my people', 'You are my people' (2:23).
God will have mercy on 'no mercy' and say to 'not my people', 'You are my people'.
Hosea buys back his unfaithful wife, a picture of Israel returning in the latter days to seek the LORD and 'David their king'.
Those once far off are brought near by the blood of Christ.
Paul says God has called vessels of mercy 'not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles', and quotes Hosea 2:23 and 1:10 as the proof.
Peter tells his readers: once you were not a people, but now you are God's people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have.
'They will be his people, and God himself will be with them': the covenant formula is fulfilled for the whole redeemed humanity.

Hosea prophesied in the northern kingdom in the eighth century BC, before Samaria fell to Assyria in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:6). Assyria resettled the northern Israelites among the nations and brought foreigners into Samaria (2 Kings 17:24), so the 'not my people' became mixed among the Gentiles. Paul wrote Romans about AD 57 to a church of Jewish and Gentile believers in Rome, where Jews had been expelled under Claudius about AD 49 and had since returned (Acts 18:2). 1 Peter's readers in Asia Minor seem to have been largely Gentile (1 Peter 1:18; 4:3), though this is disputed.

The fulfilment reading holds that Gentile believers are the 'not my people' who have become 'my people' and 'children of the living God'. This is one of the clearest places where the New Testament applies a promise made to Israel directly to Gentiles. Christians therefore receive Israel's covenant titles (1 Peter 2:9-10: chosen race, royal priesthood, holy nation) by mercy, not by birth.

Dispensationalists such as Vlach note that in Hosea the promise concerns the northern tribes of Israel, and that Hosea 1:11 and 3:5 add a reunited people under David in the land. They hold that Paul and Peter use Hosea by analogy: the same God who calls rejected Israel 'my people' can call Gentiles who were never his people. The Gentile application shows God's character but does not remove the original promise to ethnic Israel, which remains for a future national restoration.

Fulfilment writers answer that Paul introduces the text as 'as indeed he says in Hosea' (Romans 9:25), which grounds his claim, not merely illustrates it. Since the northern tribes were scattered and mixed among the nations, some writers see the Gentile mission as gathering the very people Hosea described. Either way, the New Testament treats the Hosea promise as now being fulfilled in a mixed Jewish-Gentile church.

Dispensationalists reply that Paul next turns to Isaiah's remnant texts for Israel (Romans 9:27-29), keeping a distinction between Israel and the Gentiles inside the argument. They point out that Romans 11:1-2 denies that God has rejected his people, which they take as a continuing national promise beside the Gentile one.
The remnant will return

In the day of Assyria's judgment, 'a remnant will return' (shear yashub), the remnant of Jacob, to the mighty God. Though Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant will return; destruction is decreed, overflowing with righteousness (Isaiah 10:20-22). The name of Isaiah's son Shear-jashub (Isaiah 7:3) means 'a remnant will return'.
A remnant of Jacob will return to the mighty God.
In Elijah's day God kept seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal; Paul uses this example in Romans 11:4.
Jesus calls his disciples 'little flock' and promises them the kingdom; the faithful remnant gathers around him.
Paul quotes Isaiah 10:22: though Israel's number be as the sand of the sea, only the remnant will be saved.
'At the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace'; Paul himself, an Israelite of Benjamin, is evidence (11:1).
'And in this way all Israel will be saved'; how the remnant relates to 'all Israel' is the central question of the debate.

Isaiah spoke during the Assyrian crisis, when the north fell (722 BC) and Sennacherib invaded Judah in 701 BC, taking many cities and besieging Jerusalem, as his own annals (the Taylor Prism) also record. Only Jerusalem survived, 'a remnant' (2 Kings 19:30-31). In the first century, the Jewish believers in Jesus numbered 'many thousands' in Jerusalem (Acts 21:20), but most of the nation's leaders rejected him, and Paul wrestles with this in Romans 9-11 about AD 57, a decade before the war with Rome.

On the fulfilment reading, the true Israel has always been the believing remnant within the nation, and Gentiles are grafted into that remnant (Romans 11:17). The church is not a new people replacing Israel but the faithful remnant of Israel enlarged with Gentiles. This keeps believers humble: they stand by faith, not by birth (Romans 11:20).

Dispensationalists see the present Jewish remnant in the church as a pledge that God has not finished with Israel as a nation. Paul says Israel's 'fullness' (11:12) and 'acceptance' (11:15) will bring 'life from the dead' to the world, and that a partial hardening lasts 'until' the fullness of the Gentiles comes in (11:25). They read 'all Israel' in 11:26 as the nation at the end of the age, turning to Christ at his return.

Fulfilment writers are divided here. Robertson and many amillennialists read 'and in this way' (houtos, 11:26) as describing the manner: all the elect of Israel are saved through history as remnant after remnant believes alongside the Gentiles. Others in the Reformed tradition, such as Hodge, Vos and John Murray, expect a future large-scale turning of ethnic Jews to Christ, but without a restored national kingdom or a separate land program. Both hold that any future conversion brings Jews into the one olive tree, the church.

Dispensationalists answer that the 'until' of 11:25 and the contrast between Israel's present 'trespass' and future 'fullness' (11:12) imply a change of condition for the same Israel that is now hardened, that is, ethnic Israel. They welcome the Murray-Vos reading as partial agreement and argue that Romans 11:28-29 ('the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable', said of those who are now enemies of the gospel) points to more than individual conversion.
Zion, the mother city of the nations

Psalm 87 names Rahab (Egypt), Babylon, Philistia, Tyre and Cush among those who know the LORD, and says of each, 'this one was born there'; the LORD registers the peoples as born in Zion (Psalms 87:4-6). Isaiah 60 sees nations coming to Zion's light, its gates open day and night to receive their wealth, and the LORD himself as its everlasting light so that sun and moon are no longer needed (Isaiah 60:3, 60:11, 60:19).
Of Zion it will be said that this one and that one were born in her, and the Most High establishes her.
David captures the stronghold of Zion, which becomes the city of David and the seat of the Davidic king (Psalms 2:6).
Jesus enters Jerusalem as the king who comes to the daughter of Zion, humble and riding on a donkey (Zechariah 9:9).
Paul says 'the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother', contrasting it with 'the present Jerusalem' which is in slavery with her children (4:25).
Believers have come to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to the assembly of the firstborn enrolled in heaven, which echoes the registry of Psalm 87.
John sees the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven; it has no need of sun or moon, for the glory of God is its light (21:23), as Isaiah 60:19 foretold.

Zion was the Jebusite fortress that David took around 1000 BC. After the exile, Nehemiah rebuilt the walls in 445/444 BC in 52 days (Nehemiah 6:15), and Herod the Great later made Jerusalem one of the grand cities of the East. Paul wrote Galatians (late 40s or early 50s AD, disputed) against teachers who pressed Gentile believers to take on circumcision, and he called the earthly Jerusalem of his day a city 'in slavery'. In AD 70 the Romans under Titus destroyed the city and temple; after the Bar Kokhba revolt (AD 132-135) Hadrian refounded it as the Roman colony Aelia Capitolina and barred Jews from it.

On the fulfilment reading, every believer, whatever their birth, is enrolled as 'born in Zion' and is a citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem (Philippians 3:20; Ephesians 2:19). Christians come to Zion now in worship, and they wait for the city that will come down at the end. Love for Zion means love for the people of God from every nation, gathered around the King.

Dispensationalists hold that Isaiah 60 describes a restored earthly Jerusalem in the millennium: foreigners rebuild its walls (60:10), the descendants of its oppressors bow at its feet (60:14), and it is called 'the City of the LORD, the Zion of the Holy One of Israel' (60:14). They see the heavenly Jerusalem of Revelation 21 as the eternal city after the millennium, distinct from the earthly capital of the thousand years. Many see the reunification of Jerusalem under Israeli rule in 1967 as connected with Luke 21:24 ('until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled'), though others in the camp are cautious about such links.

Fulfilment writers reply that Revelation 21-22 quotes Isaiah 60 again and again (the light, the open gates, the nations' glory), which places its fulfilment in the new Jerusalem rather than an intermediate city. Paul's contrast of the 'present Jerusalem' and the 'Jerusalem above' (Galatians 4:25-26) leaves no theological future for the earthly city as such. Psalm 87 already sees Zion as a city whose citizens are born from the nations, which is the church's identity.

Dispensationalists answer that Revelation 21 can draw on Isaiah 60 for the eternal state while Isaiah 60's details of foreign kings, enemies bowing and walls built by foreigners fit an earthly age better. They argue that Galatians 4 is about two covenants (law and promise), not about the future of Jerusalem as a place, and point to Jesus' words that Jerusalem will not see him 'until' it says 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord' (Matthew 23:39).

While praying about Jeremiah's seventy years, Daniel is told by Gabriel that seventy 'sevens' are decreed for his people and his holy city: to finish transgression, end sins, atone for iniquity, bring in everlasting righteousness, seal vision and prophet, and anoint a most holy place (Daniel 9:24). From a word to restore Jerusalem to an anointed one there will be seven and sixty-two sevens; then an anointed one will be cut off, and the people of a coming prince will destroy the city and sanctuary (9:25-26). 'He' will confirm a covenant with many for one seven and in the middle of it end sacrifice and offering, with an abomination that desolates (9:27).
Six goals are set within seventy sevens for Daniel's people and holy city.
The jubilee came after seven sevens of years; seventy sevens are ten jubilees, a final release beyond the seventy years of exile (Jeremiah 25:11).
Jesus begins his ministry announcing 'the time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God has come near'.
Jesus speaks of 'my blood of the covenant, poured out for many', which fulfilment writers connect with the covenant confirmed 'with many' (Daniel 9:27).
Christ has appeared once at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself, the 'end of sins' and 'atonement for iniquity' of Daniel 9:24.
Jesus refers to 'the abomination of desolation spoken of by the prophet Daniel'; fulfilment writers place it in AD 66-70 (compare Luke 21:20), futurists in a coming tribulation.

Gabriel's word came in the first year of Darius the Mede (Daniel 9:1), about 539 BC. Possible starting points are Cyrus' decree (538 BC, Ezra 1:1-4), Artaxerxes' commission to Ezra (458/457 BC, Ezra 7), and Artaxerxes' permission to Nehemiah to rebuild the city (445/444 BC, Nehemiah 2:1-8). From 457 BC, 483 years reach about AD 26-27, near Jesus' baptism; Sir Robert Anderson and later Harold Hoehner counted from 444 BC with 360-day prophetic years to AD 32 or 33. Jesus was crucified about AD 30 or 33, and Roman legions under Titus destroyed the city and temple in AD 70, as Daniel 9:26 described.

The fulfilment reading (Young, Kline, Robertson, Gentry) holds that the six goals of 9:24 are accomplished by Christ's death and resurrection: sin ended, atonement made, everlasting righteousness brought in. The 'he' of 9:27 is the Messiah, who confirms the covenant with many and makes the temple sacrifices obsolete by his own sacrifice, while the 'people of the prince', the Romans, destroy the city in AD 70. Believers live in the righteousness that Daniel's weeks promised, and the fall of the temple shows that sacrifice has ended for ever.

Dispensationalists (Walvoord, Pentecost, Hoehner, Ice) argue that the sixty-nine weeks ended at Jesus' triumphal entry or crucifixion, after which the prophetic clock stopped. Verse 26 places the cutting off of Messiah and the destruction of AD 70 'after' the sixty-two weeks, not inside the seventieth, so a gap is in the text. The 'he' of 9:27 is the nearest antecedent, 'the prince who is to come', a future Antichrist who will make a seven-year treaty with Israel and break it in the middle, matching the 42 months and 1,260 days of Revelation 11:2 and 12:6 and the man of lawlessness in the temple (2 Thessalonians 2:4).

Fulfilment writers answer that nothing in the text suggests a gap of two thousand years inside a numbered sequence, and that the main subject of 9:25-26 is the Messiah, not the prince, who is only mentioned in a phrase about his 'people'. Confirming a covenant 'with many' fits the new covenant (Isaiah 53:11-12 'he shall justify many'; Matthew 26:28), not a peace treaty, and Jesus' ministry of about three and a half years before his death fits 'the middle of the week'. Some (Kline) read the seventieth week symbolically as stretching through the church age to the end.

Futurists reply that Jesus placed the abomination of desolation in the future in his own teaching (Matthew 24:15), and the events after it include his coming in glory (24:29-31), which did not happen in AD 70. The six goals of 9:24 include 'to seal up vision and prophecy' and full everlasting righteousness for Daniel's people and city, which they argue are not yet complete for Israel. Prophetic gaps elsewhere (Isaiah 61:1-2 read by Jesus in Luke 4:18-19, stopping before 'the day of vengeance') show the pattern is not foreign to Scripture.
They will look on him whom they pierced

God will pour out on the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and supplication, and they will look on 'me whom they have pierced' and mourn for him as for an only son (Zechariah 12:10). The mourning is likened to the mourning for Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo (12:11), and on that day a fountain will be opened for sin and uncleanness (13:1).
Jerusalem will look on the pierced one and mourn, after God pours out a spirit of grace.
The great lament for King Josiah, killed at Megiddo, became a lasting national mourning, the pattern Zechariah 12:11 recalls.
After the soldier pierces Jesus' side, John says 'another Scripture says, They will look on him whom they pierced'.
At Pentecost, after the Spirit is poured out, Jerusalem's crowds are 'cut to the heart' about the Jesus they crucified (2:36) and about 3,000 repent.
The blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin, the fountain of Zechariah 13:1 opened for believers.
He comes with the clouds, every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all the tribes of the earth (or land) will mourn.

Zechariah prophesied in Jerusalem from 520 BC (Zechariah 1:1), encouraging the rebuilding of the second temple under Zerubbabel. The mourning for Josiah, killed by Pharaoh Neco at Megiddo in 609 BC (2 Kings 23:29), was still remembered as the nation's great grief. Jesus was crucified by Roman soldiers at the request of Jerusalem's leaders around AD 30 or 33, and John, writing later in the century, presents himself as the eyewitness of the piercing (John 19:35). Revelation, dated either before AD 70 or about AD 95 (disputed), applies the text to Christ's coming.

The fulfilment reading holds that the piercing was fulfilled at the cross and the looking and mourning began at Pentecost, when the Spirit of grace was poured out and Jews in Jerusalem repented. Every believer has 'looked' on the pierced one in faith and found the cleansing fountain. Revelation 1:7 widens the circle: at his coming all will see him, and those who did not repent will mourn in judgment.

Dispensationalists (Fruchtenbaum, Walvoord, Ice) read Zechariah 12-14 as one end-time scene: all nations gather against Jerusalem (12:2-3, 12:9), God defends the city, and the nation as a whole, by families and clans (12:12-14), turns to the Messiah at his visible return. They connect this to Hosea 5:15, Matthew 23:39 and Romans 11:26 as Israel's national confession that precedes or accompanies the second coming. John 19:37 fulfils the piercing; the national mourning is still future.

Fulfilment writers answer that John explicitly ties the text to the crucifixion, and Acts shows the outpouring of the Spirit and the mourning of Jerusalem's people in Acts 2. Preterists read Revelation 1:7's 'tribes of the land' as Judea's tribes seeing Christ's coming in the judgment of AD 70; amillennialists see the final universal coming, when all, including the unrepentant, will mourn. Neither reading needs a distinct national conversion inside a future political state.

Dispensationalists reply that Acts 2 involved thousands, not the clan-by-clan mourning of the whole house of David and of Jerusalem in 12:12-14. They hold that the setting, with all nations besieging Jerusalem and God destroying them (12:9), did not occur at Pentecost or at AD 70, when Jerusalem fell rather than being rescued. Some fulfilment writers in the Murray-Vos line grant a future large-scale Jewish turning, which narrows the gap between the camps.
His feet on the Mount of Olives

Zechariah 14 describes a day of the LORD when the nations gather against Jerusalem, the city is taken and half its people go into exile (14:1-2). Then the LORD fights for his people: his feet stand on the Mount of Olives, which splits from east to west, living waters flow from Jerusalem to east and west (14:8), and the LORD becomes king over all the earth (14:9). The survivors of the nations go up yearly to worship the King and keep the feast of Booths (14:16), and even the bells of the horses bear 'Holy to the LORD' (14:20).
The LORD will be king over all the earth; on that day the LORD will be one and his name one.
The glory of the LORD left the temple and stood on the mountain east of the city, the Mount of Olives; Zechariah sees the LORD return to the same place.
Jesus ascends from the Mount of Olives (called Olivet), and the angels say he will come in the same way as they saw him go.
On the last great day of the feast of Booths, when water rites recalled the hope of Zechariah 14:8, Jesus offers rivers of living water: the Spirit.
A river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and there is no more curse, which echoes Zechariah 14:8 and 14:11.

Zechariah 9-14 is undated and its date is disputed, though many place it in the Persian period after 520 BC. The Mount of Olives lies east of Jerusalem across the Kidron valley. Jesus taught there about Jerusalem's fall (Mark 13:3), wept over the city from its slope (Luke 19:37-41) and ascended from it (Acts 1:12). In the siege of AD 70 Titus stationed the Tenth Legion on the Mount of Olives (Josephus, Jewish War 5.70), and the city was taken and its people killed or exiled, which preterist readers compare with Zechariah 14:1-2.

Both camps agree the chapter points to the LORD's universal kingship, which believers already confess in Jesus as Lord of all (Acts 10:36). On the fulfilment reading, the living waters already flow through the Spirit (John 7:38) and the universal holiness of 14:20-21 is pictured in the church as God's temple and completed when the whole new Jerusalem is holy. Christians wait with hope for the visible return of the King who left from Olivet.

Dispensationalists read the chapter literally: at the end of the tribulation the nations besiege Jerusalem, Jesus returns bodily to the Mount of Olives (as Acts 1:11-12 implies), the mountain physically splits, a river flows from Jerusalem to the Dead Sea and the Mediterranean, and Christ reigns from Jerusalem in the millennium. The yearly pilgrimage for Booths, with punishment of drought on nations that refuse (14:17-19), shows a world where sin and death still exist, which fits the millennium and not the eternal state. Writers such as Walvoord and Fruchtenbaum note that a fault line runs through the area.

Fulfilment writers give two main readings. Many amillennialists treat Zechariah 14 as apocalyptic imagery of the final victory of God, using Israel's feasts and geography to picture a renewed world, fulfilled at Christ's return and in the new creation where the river of life flows (Revelation 22:1). Preterists such as Gentry and Chilton see 14:1-2 as the Roman siege of AD 70, followed by the spread of the gospel (living waters to east and west) and the nations worshipping the King. Both note that Acts 1:11 speaks of the manner of his coming (visible, with clouds) rather than a geological event, and that John 7 already links the feast of Booths' water to the Spirit.

Dispensationalists answer that the angels speak at the same mountain, and Luke takes care to name it (Acts 1:12), which strengthens a literal link with Zechariah 14:4. They argue that a siege that ends with God defeating the attackers (14:3, 14:12) cannot describe AD 70, when Rome won, and that the punishment of nations that refuse to keep Booths makes no sense in a sinless new creation. This, they say, requires an intermediate earthly kingdom.
Eden: the first sanctuary-land

God places the man in a garden in Eden 'to work it and keep it', the same pair of verbs later used for the priests' service in the tabernacle (Numbers 3:7-8). Beale and others read Eden as the first temple-land, and Adam was told to fill and subdue the whole earth (Genesis 1:28), so God's dwelling was meant to spread to the ends of the earth. Exile from Eden (Genesis 3:23-24) is the first loss of land, and every later land promise answers it.
Canaan promised to Abraham

God promises Abraham's offspring the land from the river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates, and later gives it as 'an everlasting possession' (Genesis 17:8). The promise is made inside a wider one: all families of the earth will be blessed in Abraham (Genesis 12:3). Yet Abraham himself owned only a burial cave at Machpelah (Genesis 23), a sign that the promise looked beyond his lifetime.
The land given under Joshua and Solomon

After the conquest, Joshua records that the LORD gave Israel all the land he swore to their fathers, and 'not one word failed' of all his good promises. Under Solomon, Judah and Israel were as many as the sand of the sea, and Solomon ruled from the Euphrates to the border of Egypt (1 Kings 4:20-21), matching Genesis 15:18 and 22:17. Fulfilment writers stress these texts as evidence that the land promise was kept in history; dispensationalists answer that the borders were not held permanently and that Solomon's rule was over subject kingdoms, so a final possession remains.
The prophets enlarge the vision

After exile, Isaiah tells Zion to enlarge the place of her tent, because her offspring will possess the nations and spread to the right and the left. The royal psalms already promised the king 'the nations as your heritage and the ends of the earth as your possession' (Psalms 2:8) and a rule 'from sea to sea, and from the River to the ends of the earth' (Psalms 72:8). Here the borders of Canaan start to widen into the whole world, under the Davidic king.
Heir of the world; the meek inherit the earth

Paul says the promise to Abraham and his offspring was that he would be 'heir of the world', through the righteousness of faith. Jesus takes Psalms 37:11 ('the meek shall inherit the land') and says 'the meek shall inherit the earth' (Matthew 5:5). Fulfilment writers such as Robertson, Martin and Burge see this as the New Testament's own statement that Canaan was a type of the whole earth; dispensationalists such as Vlach and Horner reply that the whole includes the part, so the widening does not cancel Israel's particular land.
A better, heavenly country

Hebrews says the patriarchs died in faith without receiving what was promised, confessing they were strangers and exiles on the earth, seeking a homeland. They desired 'a better country, that is, a heavenly one', and God has prepared a city for them (11:16), the city with foundations whose builder is God (11:10). Even while living in Canaan, Abraham looked beyond it, so the patriarchs themselves read the land promise as pointing higher.

John sees a new heaven and a new earth, and the new Jerusalem coming down from God; the dwelling place of God is with people, and he will dwell with them. The city is a cube (21:16) like the Most Holy Place, so the whole renewed world becomes God's sanctuary, and the river and tree of life return from Eden (22:1-2). Both camps agree the story ends here; they differ on whether an earthly millennial kingdom centred on Israel's land comes first, and on whether the renewed earth keeps a special place for the land of Israel.

Three separate questions are often tangled together when Christians speak about the modern State of Israel, and this section keeps them apart. First, a theological question: is the founding of the state in 1948, and events since, a fulfilment of biblical prophecy? Christians answer this differently, and both answers are set out below with their best arguments. Second, a historical question: how did the state actually come into being? Here the record is largely agreed: a mostly secular national movement (Zionism) born in late nineteenth-century Europe, British imperial decisions (the Balfour Declaration and the Mandate), the catastrophe of the Holocaust, a United Nations vote in 1947, and the outcome of the 1948-49 war, which also displaced some 700,000 Palestinian Arabs. Third, a moral question: the dignity, safety and worth of the Jewish people. That question does not depend on the answer to the first. A Christian may hold that 1948 is not a fulfilment of prophecy and still honour the Jewish people, oppose antisemitism, and affirm the right of every people, Jewish and Palestinian, to live in safety. A Christian may hold that it is a fulfilment and still care for justice for Palestinians, many of whom are Christians. This study takes no side on current political or military disputes.
